name: cosmos.gl (@cosmos.gl/graph)
what: GPU WebGL force-graph engine; layout and drawing run in shaders, so the CPU is not the bottleneck. Engine behind Cosmograph. Hover, click, right-click/long-press, pinch zoom, fitView, point-clustering force (v2), collision force (v3).
why_it_matters: Only open-source option found that claims to draw the full 339k-node / ~900k-edge person-work graph interactively without a server-side layout. Best candidate for an overview of the whole graph where an ego view is not enough.
numbers: README: 'hundreds of thousands of points and links on modern hardware' (github.com/cosmosgl/graph). 1.3k stars, 86 forks (same page). OpenJS blog claims over one million nodes and links (https://openjsf.org/blog/introducing-cosmos-gl), vendor claim, untested. iOS/Android WebGL extension gaps noted in search summary.
ui_notes: Steal the clustering force: setPointClusters / setPointClusterStrength pulls people sharing a topic into visible groups without pre-computed layouts. Hover highlights the topmost overlapping point and skips GPU work when the mouse is still.
note: MIT (repo LICENCE file and README, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api cosmosgl/graph: 1,296 stars, 86 forks, MIT (row 1.3k / 86 forks, correct).

name: Cosmograph
what: Browser network and embedding explorer built on cosmos.gl, with DuckDB-Wasm for in-browser filter and aggregate and Mosaic for pre-aggregated cached updates. Intended for exploring networks and AI embeddings.
why_it_matters: Shows the architecture we would want: keep the data in an in-browser columnar store, aggregate on filter, and push only the visible subset to the GPU renderer.
numbers: Docs: GPU layouts for 'hundreds of thousands or millions of nodes and links' in seconds (vendor claim). Docs also say most CPU force layouts 'hit performance walls around 50,000 nodes' (cosmograph.app/docs-general/concept/). No hard limit stated.
ui_notes: Filter + histogram + timeline panels drive a GPU graph; selection in one panel filters the others. Pattern worth copying: aggregate in DuckDB/Mosaic, render only the filtered subset.
note: LICENCE CONFLICT, unresolved. Search summary says @cosmograph/cosmos is CC-BY-NC-4.0 (non-commercial, contact maintainers for commercial use); the concept page does not state a licence and its Citing and licensing page was not fetched. Do not ship @cosmograph/* without confirming. The cosmos.gl engine underneath is MIT.

name: sigma.js (v3, v4-beta)
what: WebGL graph renderer built on graphology. Node programs for image, border, pie-chart nodes (companion packages), map backgrounds via Leaflet/MapLibre, @sigma/layer-webgl for custom WebGL layers. Hover, click, label rendering and node/edge reducers for highlight and dimming.
why_it_matters: Default choice for an ego-network view (a few hundred nodes, interactive, with graphology doing the data work). Mature, MIT, large community.
numbers: 12.2k stars, 1.6k forks (github.com/jacomyal/sigma.js). Tagline: 'visualizing graphs of thousands of nodes and edges'. No official numeric ceiling on the page. Knogin.com marketing page claims 100k nodes at 30-60 fps; unverified, treat as anecdotal (https://knogin.com/developers/sigma-large-graph-rendering).
ui_notes: Use reducers (nodeReducer/edgeReducer) to dim everything outside the selected ego ring instead of hiding it. Keeps spatial memory while expanding. Edge drawing is the cost; cap visible edges.
note: MIT (LICENSE.txt in repo, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api jacomyal/sigma.js: 12,187 stars, 1,618 forks, MIT (row 12.2k / 1.6k, correct).

name: graphology
what: Graph data model for JS/TS (directed, undirected, mixed, multi). Event emitter used as sigma.js backend. Standard library with layouts (ForceAtlas2 etc.), traversals, generators and a metrics package (density, etc.). Community detection is a separate package (graphology-communities-louvain).
why_it_matters: The data layer for a browser explorer: load the 900k person-work edges once, compute degree, neighbourhoods and Louvain communities in a worker, and feed sigma. Also lets us prototype clustering off the server.
numbers: 1.8k stars (github.com/graphology/graphology). No published node-count benchmark on the repo page; treat 339k nodes as untested and benchmark ourselves.
ui_notes: Use graph events (nodeAdded, edgeAdded) to drive incremental expansion: each click adds neighbours to the same graph instead of reloading.
note: MIT (LICENSE.txt, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api graphology/graphology: 1,760 stars, 117 forks, MIT (row 1.8k, correct).

name: Gephi Lite
what: Browser version of Gephi. Runs with no server; data stays on the user's machine; optional save/load via GitHub Gists. Built on sigma.js and graphology. Open a GEXF file from a URL, embed in iFrame or drive with a JS driver. Lighter than desktop Gephi: smaller networks, fewer operations.
why_it_matters: Reference for a no-server exploration tool with layouts, filters and statistics in the browser. Also a link-out target: we can export GEXF and let power users open it.
numbers: 354 stars (github.com/gephi/gephi-lite). No published node limit found; the repo does not state one. Developers describe it as for 'smaller networks' (publicdatalab.org interview).
ui_notes: Left-panel filter and ranking stack (attribute filters, partition colouring, ranking size) with live preview. Good model for a people-graph filter sidebar.
note: GPL-3.0 (README and sidebar). Copyleft: reuse the idea or link out, do not copy code into a non-GPL repo. | check: gh api gephi/gephi-lite: 354 stars, 48 forks, licence GPL-3.0 (row 354 correct; licence not stated in row).

name: react-force-graph (2D, 3D, VR, AR)
what: React wrappers over force-graph (2D canvas), 3d-force-graph (ThreeJS/WebGL), VR (A-Frame) and AR (AR.js) with identical interfaces. Click, hover and drag handlers; autoPauseRedraw stops canvas redraw when layout settles.
why_it_matters: Fastest path to a working React explorer prototype for a few thousand nodes (ego view or a topic cluster). Not the right tool for 339k nodes in 2D canvas.
numbers: 3.3k stars (github.com/vasturiano/react-force-graph). No node-count limit stated. cooldownTime defaults to 15000 ms. enablePointerInteraction is 'at the cost of performance' (README).
ui_notes: autoPauseRedraw plus cooldownTime gives the settle-then-freeze feel; use it for ego views so the layout stops moving and the user can read labels.
note: MIT (README licence section, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api vasturiano/react-force-graph: 3,324 stars, 357 forks, MIT (row 3.3k, correct).

name: Cytoscape.js
what: Graph theory library with an optional renderer for interactive graphs. Compound nodes, many layouts and an extensions ecosystem (70 listed). Tests in Mocha and Playwright; monthly feature releases.
why_it_matters: Mature option with compound (nested) nodes, which fit a person -> organisation or topic -> sub-topic hierarchy for collapsing clusters. Canvas-based, so good for thousands, not hundreds of thousands.
numbers: 11.2k stars, 1.7k forks (github.com/cytoscape/cytoscape.js). No large-graph figures on the repo page; benchmark script exists (npm run benchmark) with no published results.
ui_notes: Compound nodes: collapse a topic cluster into one parent node, expand on double-click. Same idea as cluster-to-supernode.
note: MIT (repo licence section, fetched 2026-10-14). | check: gh api cytoscape/cytoscape.js: 11,237 stars, 1,680 forks, MIT (row 11.2k / 1.7k, correct).

name: Kumu
what: Hosted relationship-mapping and stakeholder-map SaaS with a visual editor, views/filters and storytelling. Renders in WebGL (faster, less visual variety) or other modes.
why_it_matters: Benchmark for non-technical 'map' UX: named views, filter by element type, and story-mode walk-throughs. Not a fit for 339k nodes; no self-host for free tier.
numbers: Docs: no hard limit on elements, connections or maps; 'practical limit that will be different for each Kumu user'; animation and loading slow down with large imports (no figure given). Third-party FreeTier listing: $9/month and $20/month per project (unverified; check kumu.io/pricing).
ui_notes: Views as saved filter presets (show only some element types, hide the rest). Story mode steps through a curated sequence of nodes. Worth copying for curated 'stories' on the explore page.
note: Proprietary SaaS; free tier limits per the FreeTier listing, unverified.

name: Oligrapher (LittleSis)
what: JavaScript app for annotated network maps built from LittleSis data (who-knows-who in business and government). Click-through annotation series to tell a story; drag nodes and edges; force-directed or preset layouts; undo/redo; export SVG or JPEG; import from LittleSis and other APIs.
why_it_matters: Closest existing pattern to 'curated walk-through of a network': a person-centred story with annotated steps. Directly relevant to making the people graph readable for non-experts.
numbers: 112 stars, 1,438 commits (github.com/public-accountability/oligrapher). No node limit stated. Maps hosted on LittleSis.org (count not checked).
ui_notes: Story mode: each step is a view with a caption; click to advance. Export SVG for sharing. Map editing in-place (drag edges to re-link).
note: GPL-3.0 (repo page, fetched 2026-10-14). Copyleft; reuse the pattern, not the code. | check: gh api public-accountability/oligrapher: 112 stars, 22 forks, GPL-3.0; row 112 stars correct; 1,438 commits not checked.

name: Obsidian graph view (and Fast 3D Graph plugin)
what: Built-in global and local note graph. Local graph = depth-limited neighbourhood of the current note with filters (tags, folders, orphans). Switched SVG to canvas per staff reply. Community plugin Fast 3D Graph renders via WebGL.
why_it_matters: Shows the everyday pattern most people already know: local depth-1/2 graph around the current item, plus filters. The global graph failing at scale is the lesson: no one can browse a full hairball.
numbers: No official cap. Forum estimates: practical ceiling roughly 5k-25k notes depending on hardware; 35k-file vault black-screened for ~5 min; 130k-note vault froze (forum reports, not official). Fast 3D Graph plugin claims ~75 fps at 20,000 nodes and handles 50,000+ (community.obsidian.md/plugins/fast-graph).
ui_notes: Local graph with depth slider and filter by folder/tag. Orphan toggle hides isolated nodes to cut clutter. Steal the depth slider as the explicit expansion control.
note: Obsidian is proprietary; Fast 3D Graph plugin licence not checked.

name: Connected Papers
what: Builds one graph around an origin paper. Candidate pool is about 50,000 papers, of which only the few dozen most similar are shown. Similarity = co-citation plus bibliographic coupling. Force-directed layout. Click a node to highlight the shortest similarity path back to the origin. Also lists prior works (frequently cited foundations) and derivative works (papers citing many of the graph members).
why_it_matters: The clearest example of hairball avoidance by construction: show a small, meaningful subgraph (~tens of nodes) from a huge corpus, not the whole corpus. Directly maps to 'ego or similarity neighbourhood of one person, limited to top-k'.
numbers: ~50,000 candidates, few dozen shown (CASRAI guide https://casrai.org/guides/connected-papers, secondary source). Node size = citation count; colour = publication year. Exact similarity weighting not published.
ui_notes: Shortest-path-to-origin highlight on click; year colour ramp; separate lists for prior and derivative works. Copy: 'why is this person near that one' path highlight.
note: Proprietary; free tier and pricing not checked. The about page fetched with title only, so the mechanics rely on the secondary sources.

name: Litmaps
what: Literature map tool. Seed papers arranged on axes: x = publication year, y = citation count. Hollow nodes = suggested papers cited by the seeds. Seed maps and Discover maps (several seeds).
why_it_matters: A time-by-impact axis layout is an immediately readable 2D plot that scales to many nodes without a force layout. Good model for a people-by-year-by-work-count view.
numbers: 270M+ paper catalogue (per litmaps.com, vendor claim, via comparison page). Seed limit disputed across sources: one review says 1 seed on Seed map, 20 seeds on free Discover map. Pro tier pricing listed differently by two 2026/older sources; unverified.
ui_notes: X/Y axis encoding with hollow vs solid node styling for suggested vs known. Copy hollow-node idea to separate 'known' work from 'suggested' connections.
note: Proprietary SaaS; pricing unverified.

name: ResearchRabbit
what: Collections-based discovery tool. Start from seed papers and get recommendations for similar, earlier and later works, built from co-authors, related works and citations. Collections are ongoing and updated. Authors can appear as two nodes in collaboration views.
why_it_matters: The 'seed set -> expand by relation type' pattern: each recommendation is labelled by why it appeared (earlier, later, similar, co-author). Matches how a user would browse people via shared works.
numbers: 310M+ papers per researchrabbit.ai (vendor claim, via comparison page). Free per one review; unverified.
ui_notes: Relation-typed expansion (earlier / later / similar / co-author) as separate tabs. Copy: label every expansion by its edge type.
note: Proprietary, free to use per one review (unverified).

name: Inciteful
what: Free online citation-network explorer that builds user-defined graphs from OpenAlex, Semantic Scholar and Crossref. Seed-based expansion of a citation neighbourhood.
why_it_matters: A free, public example of the same expansion model over an open scholarly graph, relevant if we ever want to layer OpenAlex metadata on top of our people graph.
numbers: No node limit found. Official GitHub repo not located in search, so licence and code availability unknown.
ui_notes: Seed-set graph with a stated data source per edge (OpenAlex, S2, Crossref). Copy: show provenance on each edge.
note: Licence unknown; repo not found in this search.

name: Apple Embedding Atlas
what: Open-source browser and Python tool for interactive embedding maps with metadata. Automatic clustering with labels, kernel density contours, order-independent transparency for overlapping points, nearest-neighbour search from a query or a point, cross-filtering linked charts (bar, line, bubble, count plot, eCDF), multimodal viewers, MCP access. React, Svelte, Vanilla JS and Python (CLI, Jupyter, Streamlit).
why_it_matters: Strongest find for the similarity-map pattern: a 2D map of all people placed by similarity (e.g. UMAP of topic vectors) avoids edges entirely, so the 2M topic edges never reach the screen. Lasso or density-select a region, then open the ego view.
numbers: 5.0k stars, 331 forks (github.com/apple/embedding-atlas). 'Up to a few million points, powered by WebGPU' (repo page). WebGL 2 fallback per search summary. No benchmark table on the page.
ui_notes: Density contours show where people cluster; click a cluster label to zoom; cross-filter bar/bubble charts by year, role or topic. Copy the cross-filter layout for the explore page's side panels.
note: MIT (repo page, fetched 2026-10-14). WebGPU needs a recent browser; check fallback on target devices. | check: gh api apple/embedding-atlas: 4,987 stars, 331 forks, MIT (row 5.0k / 331, correct; licence is MIT).

name: Nomic Atlas
what: Hosted embedding map. Layout via UMAP below 50k points and the Nomic Project optimiser at 50k+ points (Python docs default). Metadata filter, regex and semantic lasso selection; user-supplied 2D coordinates accepted.
why_it_matters: Proof of the 2D-map-at-scale pattern for a hosted product; shows the 50k threshold where layout method switches. Useful as a reference UI, not as a dependency (proprietary, hosted).
numbers: Release notes: selections work at the 'tens of millions' scale (vendor claim, docs.nomic.ai/atlas/release-notes). Layout threshold: UMAP < 50,000 points, Nomic Project >= 50,000 (Python docs).
ui_notes: Lasso plus regex plus metadata filter in one bar. Accepting user-supplied x/y lets us push our own precomputed person coordinates.
note: Proprietary hosted service; pricing not checked.

name: deck.gl (visgl)
what: WebGL2/WebGPU layer framework from vis.gl. ScatterplotLayer for point maps; aggregation layers (hexbin, grid) for very dense point sets. Instancing gives millions of points in one draw.
why_it_matters: Right tool for the overview layer of 339k people as points with aggregation at low zoom. Pairs with a sigma ego view. Avoids edge rendering by design.
numbers: Google Maps codelab: 'hundreds of thousands' easily, 'millions' when optimised. Uber blog: 860K circles instanced (https://www.uber.com/blog/visualizing-data-sets-deck-gl-framework/). Property-assessment blog warns aggregation beats scatter at high density.
ui_notes: Aggregate at low zoom (hexbin counts), switch to individual points on zoom-in. Copy the zoom-driven level of detail.
note: Licence NOT verified from a fetched page; the search returned none. From memory it is MIT, but check github.com/visgl/deck.gl LICENSE before use. The URL given is a secondary guide.

name: Graphistry (PyGraphistry + GPU server)
what: Dataframe-native Python graph visual analytics. WebGL client renders graphs in the browser; server-side GPU analytics (RAPIDS) for larger graphs. GFQL query language with a subset of Cypher, optional GPU acceleration. Optional graph autoML (UMAP, feature engineering, GNN support).
why_it_matters: Reference for 'big graph in a browser, heavy lifting on a GPU box' split. We could keep the 339k graph on the server and stream a filtered subgraph to a WebGL client.
numbers: 2.6k stars, BSD-3-Clause (github.com/graphistry/pygraphistry). Client: up to 8MM nodes + edges at once; older client GPUs smooth at 100K-2MM elements (PyPI listing, https://pypi.org/project/graphistry/0.34.14). GPU mode '100X+ speedups' (repo). Demo 80,000+ Facebook friendships.
ui_notes: Server-side filter then client-side render; the split keeps the browser light. Copy the 'filter on server, draw subset' loop.
note: PyGraphistry BSD-3-Clause (repo sidebar). Server licence NOT stated on the page; check before self-hosting. | check: gh api graphistry/pygraphistry: 2,569 stars, BSD-3-Clause (row 2.6k, BSD-3, correct).

name: OCCRP Aleph (network diagrams and timelines)
what: Investigative data platform. Explore entities visually through network diagrams and timelines. Lets users pivot from an entity to its connections across datasets.
why_it_matters: Shows a people-plus-documents graph explored through entity pages with a timeline and a network pane side by side. Relevant to people -> works browsing.
numbers: No node-count limit found. MIT licence per IADB catalogue (https://knowledge.iadb.org/en/code-development/open-source-solutions/occrp-aleph). Aleph Pro rebuild announced (OCCRP), licence not verified. One aggregator marks one repo as dormant (unverified).
ui_notes: Entity page with linked network and timeline tabs; pivot by clicking an entity. Copy: an entity page is the unit of navigation, not the whole graph.
note: MIT per IADB catalogue and OpenAleph FAQ (secondary). Aleph Pro licence unverified.

name: Pantheon (MIT Media Lab Macro Connections, built by Datawheel)
what: Public site browsing notable people by country, city, occupation and era. Lists for People, Places and Occupations; profile pages for each; a Born on This Day feed; download and API pages; Trending profiles from Wikipedia pageviews.
why_it_matters: Browsing people by facets (occupation, country, era) instead of a graph is the browsable default for 339k people. Pantheon's facet pages are the model for our people index; the graph sits behind each profile.
numbers: Site claims data on more than 85,000 biographies (pantheon.world). Our graph: 339,217 people. Pantheon's dataset is the curated subset, not comparable on scale.
ui_notes: Facet listing pages (occupation x country combinations, eras) as entry points; profile page shows related people. Copy the occupation x country combination pages as landing pages for slices of the graph.
note: Footer links Creative Commons BY-SA 4.0 for the site content (per fetched page). Data licence and code not checked. | check: pantheon.world homepage: '85,000+ Biographies' (row 85,000, correct).

name: Histomania
what: Timeline browser for comparing events and people across history, sourced from Wikidata.
why_it_matters: Timeline as the main axis for people in time, with comparison across individuals. Matches the year dimension in our person-work edges.
numbers: No node count found. Listed on the Wikidata visualisation tools page (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Tools/Visualize_data).
ui_notes: Horizontal life-span bars per person on a shared time axis. Copy: a life-span lane view for a selected set of people.
note: Licence not checked; site-level tool.

name: Histropedia
what: Auto-generated interactive timelines built from Wikipedia and Wikidata, including a Wikidata Query Timeline app (SPARQL-driven) at js.histropedia.com.
why_it_matters: Shows that a timeline can be generated from a query, not hand-built, which we can do from our own edges (filter -> timeline).
numbers: No node count found. Listed on https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Tools/Visualize_data. Query Timeline app at https://js.histropedia.com/apps/query-timeline/.
ui_notes: Query -> timeline with category colouring and zoomable axis. Copy: the timeline is a view of the current filter, not a separate page.
note: Licence not checked.

name: Scholia
what: Wikidata front end for scholarly metadata. Publication lists per author, venue or organisation; citation bar charts; co-author graphs; topic pages built from SPARQL queries.
why_it_matters: Closest existing public example of a people-and-works graph browser: each person page has a co-author graph and a publication list. Good model for profile pages with a small ego graph.
numbers: No published node limit found. Uses Wikidata Query Service (per search summary). Listed in the Wikidata tools table (https://www.wikidata.org/wiki/Wikidata:Tools/Visualize_data).
ui_notes: Person profile = list of works plus small co-author graph; topic page = chart set. Copy the profile-first layout: graph is secondary to a list.
note: Licence not verified (GitHub URL returned 404 on fetch); assumed open source, check before reuse.

name: Wikidata visualisation tools directory (SQID, Reasonator, Graphpedia, Wikidata Graph Builder, metaphacts, and others)
what: Community list of 61 Wikidata visualisation tools. Relevant entries: SQID (browse and query with property and class usage stats), Reasonator (enhanced item display), Graphpedia (explorable knowledge graphs of properties), Wikidata Graph Builder (d3 item graph), Wikidata metaphacts (entity explorer with pathfinding between items), GeneaWiki and Wikidata Descent Map (family trees filterable by date).
why_it_matters: Pathfinding between two items and family-tree style ego views are patterns we could copy. The list gives a quick map of which ones are still live.
numbers: 61 tools listed (page count). No per-tool node limits given.
ui_notes: Pathfinding (metaphacts): pick two people, show the shortest connecting chain. Descent Map: date filter applied to a tree. Both are good patterns for a people explore page.
note: Directory page only; individual tool licences not checked. Several listed tools use legacy wmflabs hosts that may be offline.

name: Ogma (Linkurious)
what: Commercial JavaScript graph visualisation library by Linkurious (now a Nuix company). Positioned as the next step when sigma.js reaches its limits. Also the successor to the deprecated linkurious.js.
why_it_matters: Commercial answer if sigma.js stops being enough at our scale. Shows the vendor view of where sigma tops out, but that is a vendor claim.
numbers: No published node limit found. Pricing not public (free trial per Capterra listing). The old linkurious.js was dual-licensed GPLv3 plus commercial.
ui_notes: Not checked in detail; the comparison page is the only fetched source.
note: Commercial; GPL-style option was for the deprecated linkurious.js, not Ogma.
